analysis.one_liner: Lets the Postal Service offer small loans, checking and savings accounts, and money transfers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended postal law to let the U.S. Postal Service offer basic banking: small-dollar loans, checking and interest-bearing savings accounts, cheaper international money transfers, and a prepaid 'Postal Card' to use those services. The goal was to give people who lack bank accounts — or who pay steep fees to payday lenders, check cashers, and wire-transfer companies — a low-cost public alternative, with the option of partnering with banks and credit unions. It was referred to committee in July 2014 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly millions of 'unbanked' and 'underbanked' households — disproportionately lower-income — who today cash checks at storefront services, borrow from payday lenders at triple-digit annual rates, and pay high fees to send money abroad. They would gain access to basic financial services at a trusted neighborhood post office, likely at far lower cost.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes new authority into postal law for the USPS to provide small-dollar loans, checking accounts, interest-bearing savings accounts, and international money-transfer services [S2][S3].
It authorizes a 'Postal Card' — a prepaid card letting users access those financial services, including at post offices in communities where conventional banks have closed branches [S2][S3].

The bill allows the USPS to provide these services alone or in partnership with FDIC-insured banks and credit unions, so customers could get federal deposit insurance rather than only a government float [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, check-cashing outlets, and money-transfer companies would lose a large slice of their customer base — high-fee services aimed at people without bank accounts. Commercial banks would face a public competitor for low-dollar deposit and small-loan business, though the bill also opens a partnership role for banks and credit unions. Taxpayers could bear some risk if postal financial services lost money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders, check cashers, money-transfer firms

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the Postal Service broad discretion to add 'other basic financial services as appropriate in the public interest' on its own judgment, with no additional congressional guardrails specified in the bill text [S3].

The bill authorizes the USPS to make small-dollar loans without spelling out interest-rate caps, underwriting standards, or loss-absorbing capital in the bill text, so an honest supporter would acknowledge the program's safety would depend entirely on how USPS designed it — and losses could land on USPS finances, which are already strained [S3].
Banking trade groups have historically opposed government-run postal banking as unfair public competition with private banks, a policy objection known from reporting outside this record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it targets, the benefit is substantial and direct: cheaper credit, deposits, and remittances from a public institution present in nearly every zip code. The real risks are operational — USPS has no lending track record and the bill leaves program design almost entirely to the agency — so a poorly run loan program could cost the postal service money without helping the people it aims to serve. Those risks argue for careful implementation, not for leaving payday lenders and check cashers as the only option.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Cedric Richmond introduced the bill on July 23, 2014, joined by four original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform the same day [S5][S3].
Thirteen House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any recorded opposition, the clear beneficiaries were the alternative financial services industry — payday lenders, check cashers, and money-transfer firms — which kept the unbanked market and its high fees to itself. The committee that never scheduled action faced no vote on the question.

against.name: Payday lending and check-cashing industry

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; no roll call ever occurred because the bill never left committee [S4].

industries.note: The bill's small-dollar loan authority would create a direct public competitor at the post office for loans that payday lenders sell at annual rates that can run into the hundreds of percent. Borrowers' savings come out of the lenders' revenue.

Postal checking accounts, a prepaid Postal Card, and USPS international money transfers would give unbanked households an alternative to storefront check cashing and high-fee remittances — services whose business model depends on customers lacking bank access.

The bill lets USPS offer services alone, which threatens banks' low-dollar fee income, but it also explicitly authorizes partnerships with FDIC-insured depository institutions and credit unions, which could route customers and fees to participating institutions.
